A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CLEAR with the same authors, central framework, and identifiable corresponding experiments. Text extraction and rendered-page inspection support comparison of the main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments, evaluations on 17 regression datasets, and an Ames Housing case study, including detailed appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds neural-estimator experiments, separate-calibration evaluations, and measured runtime breakdowns.

M1.justification: Section 2.3 revises the stated aleatoric estimator from differences of aggregated residual quantiles to ensemble medians of nonnegative, per-member quantile gaps. The central weighted interval and calibration algorithms remain unchanged. Conformalized CLEAR was already defined in v1 Appendix G; its later experimental evaluation does not introduce that method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 17 regression datasets, synthetic homoskedastic and heteroskedastic scenarios, multivariate simulations, and Ames Housing feature settings. The neural estimators and additional calibration splits change configurations within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated DE and SQR baselines and their conformalized counterparts in Table 1 and Appendix E. Standard variant (c) gains fixed-gamma1 and fixed-lambda comparisons in Tables 22–26. The earlier UACQR-P/S results are retained unchanged in Appendix G.3 alongside standard and conformalized CLEAR, rather than removed from the paper.

E3.justification: v1 evaluates the shared validation/calibration configuration. v2 additionally evaluates 60% training, 10% validation, 10% calibration, and 20% testing splits across all three PCS variants. Appendix D.3 also introduces neural experimental configurations with distinct architectures, optimization settings, and training budgets. The original standard configuration remains.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds comparisons testing the effect of separating calibration from parameter selection. Fixed-parameter ablations are extended to variant (c), and Appendix F.5 adds component-level runtime analysis. The earlier residual-modeling, model-choice, extrapolation, and housing analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark means and standard deviations across 10 seeds, retain the nine-run exception for one naval-propulsion configuration, and report calibration parameters using median and range. Additional result tables follow these practices; changed uncertainty values do not establish a statistical-procedure change.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive neural, separate-calibration, fixed-parameter, and runtime results. Retained scores also receive numerical updates: CLEAR (a)'s insurance NCIW changes from 0.306 ± 0.032 in v1 Table 9 to 0.303 ± 0.029 in v2 Table 15. Results from the new configurations are additional evidence, not same-setting performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: The original coverage lemmas are retained, but v2 adds mathematical counterexamples concerning interval-width optimization and conditional calibration (Examples B.3–B.6), Bayesian predictive-quantile reasoning and Example B.7, and an explicitly unproved CQR extrapolation hypothesis (B.8). These substantially expand the mathematical analysis.

C1.justification: The central claims of dual-parameter calibration, residual-based aleatoric estimation, combining PCS with CQR, and compatibility with arbitrary estimator pairs remain. The new neural results provide additional support for the estimator-agnostic applicability already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands discussion of exchangeability, distribution shift, and the limits of marginal guarantees in Appendix B.1.1. Appendices B.3 and I.1 qualify the earlier favorable interpretation of NCIW by explaining how minimizing width can undermine conditional calibration. New Bayesian and runtime discussions further develop the method's motivation and applicability.

D1.justification: Appendix D.3 supplies neural architectures, diversity strategies, losses, optimization parameters, and stopping rules. Appendix F.5 newly reports hardware, memory, parallelism, and component runtimes. The existing code-access link is retained; moving it to a footnote does not change availability.

R1.justification: Appendix A gains substantial positioning against other calibration methods, distributional regression, MAQR, credal approaches, and uncertainty methods for pretrained models and image generation. It explains additional distinctions and possible integrations with CLEAR. Several time-series references are removed, while the foundational PCS/CQR/UACQR discussion remains.

P1.justification: The appendix organization changes substantially: coverage theory moves from G to B, algorithm details become B.5, and simulations, implementation details, and result configurations are regrouped. Main-text data subsections are merged, several explanations and the conclusion are tightened, and the appendix narrative gains extensive metric and theoretical discussion.

P2.justification: v2 adds a main-text neural comparison table and extensive neural, runtime, and separate-calibration tables. Variant (c)'s comparator columns are restructured, while UACQR results are redisplayed in Appendix G.3. Existing figures and the housing and abbreviation tables are retained, with some relocation and caption revisions.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important empirical gaps by testing modularity with neural estimators and evaluating the separate-calibration variant that v1 only developed theoretically. Runtime breakdowns and explicit analysis of NCIW's limitations further improve transparency and interpretation. Some editorial inconsistencies remain, notably A.1 directing UACQR claims to tables now containing fixed-parameter ablations, but the retained UACQR results in G.3 remain verifiable and these issues do not outweigh the substantial gains.
